449.title: Share your coat (Luke 3:1–20)
449.hook: John tells soldiers and tax collectors to be fair and share
449.howItsDone: Catholics hear John the Baptist's preaching in Advent, and some parishes run coat and clothing drives in winter; clothing the naked is one of the corporal works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy Jesus lost and found in the Temple, and then he grew. Your line was growing is holy. Whose growth did you name out loud? Day four hundred forty-nine, and a new week.

Luke opens chapter three like a historian dating a document. In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Pontius Pilate governor of Judea. Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the next region over, Lysanias of Abilina. Annas and Caiphas the high priests. Emperor, governor, princes, priests: a roll call of power, lined up in order. And then: the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zachary, in the desert. Not to any of them. To a man in the wilderness.
screen: `THE FIFTEENTH YEAR OF TIBERIUS.` → `A ROLL CALL OF POWER, IN ORDER.` → `THE WORD CAME TO JOHN, IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: John comes into the country around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of penance for the forgiveness of sins, just as Isaias had written: a voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the Lord. Crowds come out to be baptized, and he doesn't flatter them. Brood of vipers, he calls them. Don't tell yourselves you're safe because Abraham is your father. The axe is already laid to the root of the trees. And the crowds, shaken, ask the obvious question: then what shall we do? His answer is surprisingly ordinary. In the Douay-Rheims: "He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do in like manner." Then the publicans come, the tax collectors, and ask: and us? Don't collect more than you're supposed to. Then soldiers: and what about us? Don't bully anyone, don't accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your pay. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell the tax collectors to quit, or the soldiers to desert. He tells them to be honest and fair where they already are. The coat in his first answer is a chiton, the tunic worn under the outer cloak. If you have two, one is a spare. Give it away. John's whole preaching points past himself, to one coming who is mightier, whose sandal strap he isn't worthy to untie. And Luke ends the scene with what that honesty cost him: Herod, rebuked by John, shut him up in prison.
screen: `A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `THEN WHAT SHALL WE DO?` · `NOT QUIT: BE FAIR WHERE YOU ARE.` · `A CHITON: THE SPARE TUNIC.` · then, large: `HE THAT HATH TWO COATS, LET HIM GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your spare coat. Settle, and breathe. Picture your closet, or the hooks by your door. Go through it slowly in your mind. Somewhere in there is a coat, a sweater, a pair of shoes, something warm, that you have two of, or haven't worn in a year. Find it. See it clearly. Now think of where it could go: a shelter, a parish clothing drive, a neighbor, someone you know who's cold. Decide. Then, if you like, ask John's crowd's question about the rest of your life: what shall I do, right where I am? If you pray, offer the answer to God. The bell holds the time.
Share your coat. John the Baptist's first answer to the crowds: whoever has two coats, give one to someone who has none. Today's word.
Your line: two coats, give one. Today, take the garment you chose and put it in a bag by the door, so it actually leaves the house. Day four hundred forty-nine.

450.title: Son of Adam (Luke 3:23–38)
450.hook: Luke's family tree goes back to Adam, son of God
450.howItsDone: At every Mass the Universal Prayer, or prayers of the faithful, asks God's help for the Church, the world, and all people in need, the whole human family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, share your coat: John told the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers to be fair right where they were. Your line was two coats, give one. Did the coat leave the house? Day four hundred fifty.

Lists of names in the Bible are easy to skim. But look where Luke puts his. Jesus has just been baptized in the Jordan. The heavens open, the Holy Ghost comes down in bodily shape like a dove, and a voice from heaven says: thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased. And right there, before Jesus says a word in public, Luke stops the story for a family tree. It's not filler. Where he puts it matters, and where it ends matters more.
screen: `EASY TO SKIM.` → `THOU ART MY BELOVED SON.` → `THEN, A FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: It starts, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus himself was beginning about the age of thirty years; being (as it was supposed) the son of Joseph." As it was supposed. Luke has already told us about the angel and Mary, and he doesn't let us forget it, even here. Then the list runs backward, father by father. Heli, Matthat, and on through a long run of names, to David, to Jesse, to Judah, to Isaac, to Abraham. And then it keeps going, past Abraham, past Noah, to Seth, and to the last line: "Who was of Henos, who was of Seth, who was of Adam, who was of God." Matthew's Gospel has a family tree too, but it runs forward and starts with Abraham, the father of Israel. Luke's runs backward, all the way past Abraham, to Adam. And adam, in Hebrew, is also the ordinary word for a human being; Genesis sets it beside adamah, the ground he was formed from. So a list carries something large. Christians read it as saying that this beloved Son belongs not only to one people, but to the whole human family. Here's an honest note. Between David and Joseph, Matthew and Luke give mostly different names. The Gospels never explain why. Christian writers have proposed answers: that one list traces Joseph's line and the other Mary's, or, from an early writer named Julius Africanus, that a custom of marrying a brother's widow gave Joseph both a natural and a legal father. The Church hasn't settled on one. What both trees agree on is the point Luke ends with: son of Adam, son of God.
screen: `AS IT WAS SUPPOSED, SON OF JOSEPH.` · `BACKWARD, PAST ABRAHAM, TO ADAM.` · `ADAM: HUMAN, FROM THE GROUND.` · `TWO TREES, DIFFERENT NAMES.` · then, large: `WHO WAS OF ADAM, WHO WAS OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: widen the circle. Settle, and breathe. Start with the people closest to you: your family, whoever that is for you. Hold them for a breath. Then widen: your street, your town, the people you passed today without noticing. Then wider: strangers in cities you'll never visit, people who speak languages you don't know, people you disagree with, people you find hard to love. Luke's list runs back to one father, Adam, for all of them. If you pray, you can pray for all of them together, the whole human family. If you don't, just let the circle stay that wide for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Son of Adam. Luke's family tree for Jesus runs backward past Abraham to Adam, son of God, tying him to the whole human family. Today's word.
Your line: everyone's family. Today, look at one stranger and remind yourself, quietly: we're related. Day four hundred fifty.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of names to skip.
what it means: placed right after God calls Jesus his beloved Son, the list runs back to Adam, son of God, binding Jesus to all humanity.

451.title: The Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:16–30)
451.hook: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom to captives
451.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 4:16–21 at the Chrism Mass of Holy Week, when the bishop blesses the holy oils, and on a Sunday in Ordinary Time in the year of Luke's Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke's family tree ran back past Abraham to Adam, son of God. Your line was everyone's family. Which stranger did you remember you're related to? Day four hundred fifty-one.

After the desert, Jesus comes back to Galilee, and word about him spreads through the whole region. Then he goes home. Nazareth, where he was brought up. On the Sabbath he goes into the synagogue, as was his custom, Luke says. These are people who watched him grow up. They know his family. He stands up to read, and the attendant hands him the scroll of the prophet Isaias. He unrolls it, and finds the place he's looking for.
screen: `HOME TO NAZARETH.` → `AS WAS HIS CUSTOM.` → `THE SCROLL OF ISAIAS.`

segments.voice: He reads, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." And on: to heal the contrite of heart, to preach deliverance to the captives and sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Anointed is the root of the title Christ: Christos, the anointed one, in Hebrew Messiah. And the acceptable year of the Lord echoes the jubilee in the law of Moses, a year when land went back to its families and those sold into service went free. Then he rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down, the posture of a teacher. Every eye in the room is fixed on him. And the sermon Luke gives us is one sentence: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." At first they're impressed; they marvel at his gracious words. Then someone says: isn't this Joseph's son? And Jesus answers that no prophet is accepted in his own country. He reminds them of two old stories we read a few weeks ago: Elias was sent not to the widows of Israel but to a widow in Sarepta of Sidon; Eliseus healed not the lepers of Israel but Naaman the Syrian. God's blessing going to outsiders. The hometown crowd is filled with anger. They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill, to throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went his way. Luke puts this scene near the start of the ministry, and some readers hear it as a program for everything that follows: good news for the poor, and a welcome wider than anyone expected.
screen: `THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.` · `ANOINTED: CHRISTOS, MESSIAH.` · `THE ACCEPTABLE YEAR: A JUBILEE.` · `ISN'T THIS JOSEPH'S SON?` · then, large: `THIS DAY IS FULFILLED THIS SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Luke 4:18 aloud. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find it now, and read the verse out loud, slowly, the way Jesus read it in the synagogue. If you don't, say the phrases after this: good news to the poor. Healing for the brokenhearted. Deliverance to captives. Sight to the blind. Liberty for the bruised. Settle, and breathe. Then let each phrase land on a real person you know: someone poor, someone heartbroken, someone stuck, someone who can't see a way out. If you pray, you can hold each of them before God. The bell holds the time.
The Nazareth sermon. Jesus reads Isaiah in his hometown synagogue, says this day it is fulfilled, and is driven out when he speaks of God's blessing to outsiders. Today's word.
Your line: good news to the poor. Today, be good news to one person who's struggling: a meal, a call, an hour of your time. Day four hundred fifty-one.

fork.reveal: they're filled with anger and try to throw him down. but he, passing through the midst of them, went his way.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus read a nice verse in church.
what it means: in his own hometown, Jesus announces his mission from Isaiah, good news for the poor, and is nearly killed for saying God's welcome reaches outsiders.
what a scholar hears: the reading combines Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from 58:6; the acceptable year recalls the jubilee of Leviticus 25; Luke places it as a programmatic opening.

452.title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
452.hook: after the great catch Peter falls down: I am a sinful man
452.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's call of Peter at Sunday Mass in the year Luke's Gospel is read, and before Communion the whole congregation says aloud that they are not worthy, asking the Lord only to say the word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth and read from Isaiah. Your line was good news to the poor. Who came to mind when you heard it? Day four hundred fifty-two.

Fishermen on the lake of Genesareth worked at night, when the fish came up toward the surface. So picture the morning. Simon and his partners have been out all night and caught nothing. They're on the shore, washing their nets, tired and done. A crowd presses in on a teacher, and the teacher climbs into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little, so he can talk to the people from the water. Then, when he's finished, he says something no tired fisherman wants to hear: go back out. Put down your nets again. In the daytime. Today, what happens when Simon says yes.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `A TEACHER IN SIMON'S BOAT.` → `PUT OUT INTO THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Simon's answer is honest and a little weary: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." He goes anyway. And the nets fill so full they begin to break. He waves for the other boat, James and John, and both boats load up until they start to sink. Now, you'd expect a fisherman to celebrate. This is the best morning of his working life. Instead Luke says Simon Peter fell down at Jesus' knees, saying: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." That's today's word, and it's strange. Nobody accused Peter of anything. The catch didn't scold him. But being that close to something holy made him see himself clearly, and what he saw made him want distance. People have felt this in many places in the Bible: Isaiah in the Temple cries out that he is a man of unclean lips. And Jesus doesn't argue with Peter about whether he's a sinner. He doesn't leave, either. He says: "Fear not: from henceforth thou shalt catch men." Peter asks for distance and gets a job. Then Luke adds a quiet line: they brought their boats to land, and leaving all things, they followed him. Catholics hear an echo of this moment at every Mass. Just before Communion, the people say they are not worthy to receive the Lord, and ask him only to say the word. Those words come from a Roman centurion a little later in Luke, but the instinct is Peter's on the beach: I'm not ready for you to come this close. And the answer, in both stories, is that he comes anyway.
screen: `AT THY WORD I WILL LET DOWN THE NET.` · `THE NETS BREAK, THE BOATS SINK.` · `PETER ASKS FOR DISTANCE.` · `FEAR NOT: YOU'LL CATCH PEOPLE.` · then, large: `DEPART FROM ME, FOR I AM A SINFUL MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let God come close anyway. Settle, and breathe. Notice one thing in you that makes you want to keep God, or anyone good, at arm's length. A habit, a regret, a mood you're in today. Don't fix it. Just name it, the way Peter named his. Then picture the answer he got: not a lecture, just fear not, and an invitation to stay in the boat. Breathe with that for a while. If you pray, you can say Peter's words, and then rest in the silence after them. The bell holds the time.
Depart from me. Peter's words after the great catch, when the holy came close and he felt unworthy of it. Jesus answers with fear not. Today's word.
Your line: fear not. Today, when you catch yourself thinking you're too much of a mess for something good, say the line and stay put. Day four hundred fifty-two.

fork.reveal: he says both things at once: the honest complaint and the yes. the nets fill until they break.

what it means: being near the holy showed Peter himself, and he felt unworthy. Jesus answers with fear not and a calling.

453.title: Blessed are you poor (Luke 6:20–26)
453.hook: Luke's beatitudes are blunt, with woes to the rich
453.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's sermon on the plain at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and parishes run food pantries, Saint Vincent de Paul conferences and collections for the poor as a regular part of parish life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter at Jesus' knees in a boat full of fish, saying depart from me. Your line was fear not. Did you stay in the boat? Day four hundred fifty-three.

Matthew sets the beatitudes on a mountain: blessed are the poor in spirit. Luke tells a different scene. Jesus has spent the night praying on a mountain, picked his twelve, and then come down. He stands, Luke says, in a plain place, a level stretch of ground, with a great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon. Sick people are pushing to touch him. He lifts his eyes to his disciples and speaks. And what he says is shorter than Matthew's version, and sharper. Today, the sermon on the plain.
screen: `A NIGHT OF PRAYER, THEN DOWN.` → `A PLAIN PLACE, A GREAT CROWD.` → `SHORTER, AND SHARPER.`

segments.voice: Here is Luke's first beatitude in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." Not poor in spirit. Poor. And not they. You. Jesus is looking at real people in front of him and talking straight to them. Luke has four blessings: you poor, you who hunger now, you who weep now, you who are hated for his sake. Then he turns the coin over and gives four woes. The first: "But woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation." Woe to you that are filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you that now laugh. Woe when all men speak well of you. It's a mirror. Each blessing has its matching woe. Some readers hear woe not as a curse but as a cry of grief: alas for you. On that reading, Jesus isn't wishing harm on the comfortable. He's warning them that comfort can be the whole reward, and then it's spent. So which is it, poor or poor in spirit? Catholics read both Gospels as true and hold them together. Matthew names the heart that knows it needs God. Luke won't let that become only an inner feeling: real hunger and real poverty are what God sees first. The Catechism speaks of the Church's preferential love for the poor, and says that love is inspired by the Gospel of the beatitudes. Some saints took Luke literally. Francis of Assisi handed even his clothes back to his father, in front of the bishop, and walked away with nothing. But the line works for anyone on a Tuesday. It asks: who in your life is hungry now, or weeping now, and do you see them the way Jesus does, as blessed?
screen: `NOT POOR IN SPIRIT. POOR.` · `FOUR BLESSINGS, FOUR WOES.` · `WOE AS A CRY: ALAS FOR YOU.` · `A PREFERENTIAL LOVE FOR THE POOR.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE YE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give to someone poor today. Settle, and breathe. Think about where you'll be today and who you're likely to pass: someone outside a store, a coworker who's struggling, a family on a parish list, a food bank on your route. Pick one. Decide now what you'll give, and how: money, food, time, a real conversation. Picture handing it over and looking them in the eye, the way Jesus looked at the crowd on the plain. If you pray, you can hold that person before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Blessed are you poor. Luke's first beatitude, spoken face to face on a level plain, paired with a woe for the rich. Today's word.
Your line: blessed are you poor. Today, give one real thing to one person who needs it, and look them in the eye when you do. Day four hundred fifty-three.

454.title: Love your enemies (Luke 6:27–38)
454.hook: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over
454.howItsDone: Catholics pray for enemies in personal prayer and in the prayers of the faithful at Mass; forgiving offenses and praying for the living and the dead are among the Church's spiritual works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sermon on the plain began with blessings and woes. Your line was blessed are you poor. Who did you give to? Day four hundred fifty-four.

A grain seller dips a measuring basket. A stingy seller scoops loosely, so there's air in it. A generous one fills it, presses it down with his hands, gives it a shake so the grain settles, and fills it again until it heaps and spills over the rim. Then he pours it into the fold of your robe. You walk away with more than you paid for. Jesus ends a hard teaching with that picture. Today, what comes before it.
screen: `A MEASURING BASKET AT A STALL.` → `PRESSED, SHAKEN, SPILLING OVER.` → `POURED INTO YOUR LAP.`

segments.voice: The sermon on the plain keeps going, and it gets harder. "But I say to you that hear: Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you." Then, one after another: bless those who curse you. Pray for those who mistreat you. If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer the other. Give to everyone who asks. Do to others as you'd have them do to you. Notice that love here is not a feeling. Every item is an action: do good, bless, pray, give. Jesus doesn't ask you to like your enemy. He asks you to act for their good. Then he gives the reason: be merciful, as your Father also is merciful. God, he says, is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. And then the picture from the market: "Give, and it shall be given to you: good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom." For with the same measure that you use, it will be measured back to you. That's not a business deal. It's about the size of the basket you carry. Luke, who wrote this Gospel, also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, and he shows it happening. Stephen, dying under the stones, prays for the people throwing them. The command is hard, and Luke doesn't soften it. But it never says an enemy stops being dangerous. Loving an enemy can mean keeping a safe distance and still praying for them.
screen: `LOVE HERE IS ACTION, NOT FEELING.` · `BE MERCIFUL, AS YOUR FATHER IS.` · `THE SIZE OF YOUR BASKET.` · `STEPHEN PRAYS UNDER THE STONES.` · then, large: `GOOD MEASURE, RUNNING OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for one enemy by name. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who has hurt you or works against you. It doesn't have to be the worst one. Start small. Say their name inside, once. Notice what happens in your chest. Then, if you pray, ask God for one good thing for them: health, peace, a better day than they gave you. If you don't pray, simply wish it for them. You don't have to feel warm. You only have to do it. The bell holds the time.
Love your enemies. In Luke, love is something you do: do good, bless, pray, give, with a generous measure. Today's word.
Your line: good measure. Today, when you give anything, time, patience, a tip, an answer, press it down and let it spill over a little. Day four hundred fifty-four.

what a scholar hears: Luke ties it to God's character: be merciful (oiktirmones), as your Father is merciful, where Matthew says be perfect.

455.title: The widow of Naim (Luke 7:11–17)
455.hook: Jesus stops a funeral because he had compassion on the mother
455.howItsDone: Comforting the sorrowful is one of the Church's spiritual works of mercy, and some Catholic parishes send people to sit with grieving families, bring meals, and pray with them at the funeral vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love your enemies, and a measure of grain pressed down and spilling over. Your line was good measure. Where did you let it spill? Day four hundred fifty-five, the end of a week.

Two crowds meet at a town gate. One is coming out: a funeral, with a large crowd from the town walking beside the bier. On the bier is a young man, the only son of his mother, and she is a widow. One crowd going out with death. The other crowd is coming in, following Jesus and his disciples up the road. The town is Naim. Nobody asks Jesus for anything. Today, what he does anyway.
screen: `TWO CROWDS AT A TOWN GATE.` → `AN ONLY SON, A WIDOWED MOTHER.` → `NOBODY ASKS.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it in seven verses. Here's the turning point: "And when the Lord had seen her, being moved with mercy towards her, he said to her: Weep not." Look at the order. He sees her first. Not the dead son, the mother. Luke has already told us what is at stake for her: she is a widow, and this was her only son. Then he's moved. Luke's Greek word for it comes from the word for the inner organs, the gut. It's the feeling that grabs you in the stomach. Then he speaks to her, two words: weep not. Only then does he touch the bier, and the bearers stop. "Young man, I say to thee, arise." The young man sits up and begins to speak, and Luke adds the gentlest line in the story: he delivered him to his mother. Not to the crowd. To her. The people's reaction is fear and praise. They say a great prophet has risen among us, and God has visited his people. Readers hear an echo of Elias, who raised a widow's son at Sarephta long before, in the Third Book of Kings in the Douay. Luke is the only Gospel that tells this story, and he notices widows again and again: Anna in the Temple, the widow who keeps coming back to an unjust judge, the widow with two small coins. Catholics hear it as a picture of how God looks at grief. Before anything is fixed, someone sees you, and is moved, and speaks to you. Weep not isn't a scolding. It's what you say to a person when you're about to help.
screen: `HE SEES THE MOTHER FIRST.` · `MOVED IN THE GUT.` · `YOUNG MAN, ARISE.` · `HE GAVE HIM TO HIS MOTHER.` · then, large: `WEEP NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone grieving. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who is grieving right now: a death, a divorce, a diagnosis, a child far away. Picture them the way Jesus saw the widow at the gate. Let yourself feel it in the gut. Then decide on one small thing you'll do for them today: a message, a meal, sitting with them, saying the name of the one they lost. If you pray, hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
The widow of Naim. A mother at a town gate with her only son on the bier, seen first and comforted by Jesus before anyone asked. Today's word.

Your line: weep not. Today, reach out to one grieving person. And that's week sixty-five: two coats, the son of Adam, Nazareth, depart from me, blessed are you poor, love your enemies, and Naim. Day four hundred fifty-five.

fork.setup: you're walking into a town and meet a funeral coming out. a widow is following her only son's body. nobody has asked you for anything. what do you do?
options: step aside respectfully and let them pass.
speak to the mother first: weep not.
ask the bearers what happened.
fork.reveal: he speaks to her before he does anything else, then touches the bier and raises her son, and gives him back to her.

original.note: Greek: he was moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inner organs: mercy felt in the gut.

trapdoor: what you thought: weep not means stop crying, you're overreacting.
what it means: Jesus sees the widow, is moved, and says weep not as the first word of comfort before he raises her son.
what a scholar hears: esplanchnisthe, from splanchna, the gut; some scholars note that in the Gospels the verb is used only of Jesus or of figures in his parables.
